title: Lesson
html:
1. About this topic

In the next two assignments you write a Python program that creates one ROS 2 node. The node reads the robot's sensors and tells the robot how to move. The earlier topics explained what range sensors measure (Range Sensors) and how wheeled robots move (Locomotion). This topic adds the missing part: how a ROS 2 program receives sensor data and sends motion commands.

By the end of this topic you can:

  1. Name the parts of a ROS 2 program: node, topic, message, publisher, subscription and callback.
  2. Explain what build_node() does and why the given main() calls rclpy.spin().
  3. Find the direction of any reading in a LaserScan message from its index.
  4. Tell apart +inf, -inf and NaN in range readings, and test for them in Python.
  5. Write a Twist command for driving, turning on the spot and stopping, with the correct signs and units.
  6. Read a custom message such as the course's Flbr, and turn a written rule into a table of cases before writing code.

What you need

  • Basic Python: functions, if statements, lists and classes.
  • The Range Sensors and Locomotion topics of this course.
  • Nothing to install. Your code runs in the lab on ROS 2 Jazzy Jalisco with Python 3.12, the same versions this lesson was tested with.

2. What ROS 2 is

ROS stands for Robot Operating System. Despite the name, it is not an operating system like Windows or Linux: it is software that runs on one, and it gives robot programs a common way to exchange data. ROS 2 is the second generation. Macenski et al. (2022) describe how it was redesigned from the ground up to meet the needs of modern robots, including production-grade features that the first ROS lacked.

2.1 Nodes

A ROS 2 system is made of nodes. The ROS 2 documentation says that each node "should be responsible for a single, modular purpose", for example driving the wheel motors or publishing the data from a laser range-finder. A full robot runs many nodes at once, and they exchange data with each other.

2.2 Topics and messages

Nodes exchange data over topics. A topic is a named channel, such as /scan or /cmd_vel. The documentation describes topics as acting "as a bus for nodes to exchange messages".

  • A node that sends data on a topic has a publisher for it. A node that receives data from a topic has a subscription to it.
  • Each piece of data sent on a topic is a message. In this lab each topic name is used with one message type; for example, /scan carries sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan. To exchange messages, a publisher and a subscription must use the same topic name, the same message type and compatible Quality of Service (QoS) settings (Section 3.4).
  • A topic can connect publishers and subscriptions one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one or many-to-many. A node can publish and subscribe to any number of topics at the same time.

You can see the nodes and topics of a running ROS 2 system with the tool rqt_graph. Figure 1 is from the ROS 2 beginner tutorial, which uses the small turtlesim simulator. Nodes are drawn as ovals and topics as boxes. When you press an arrow key, the /teleop_turtle node publishes a velocity command on the topic /turtle1/cmd_vel, and the /turtlesim node subscribes to it. The tutorial's command ros2 topic info /turtle1/cmd_vel reports its type as geometry_msgs/msg/Twist, the same type your node publishes on /cmd_vel (Section 5).

A message type name has three parts: the package that defines it, the word msg, and the type. In Python you import it from the package's msg module:

from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan   # type sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist      # type geometry_msgs/msg/Twist
from rse_msgs.msg import Flbr            # the course's own type rse_msgs/msg/Flbr

2.3 The nodes in our lab

In the lab, the nodes that drive the laser and the wheels are already running. You write one node. In Assignment 1 it subscribes to /scan and publishes on /cmd_vel. In Assignment 2 it subscribes to /flbr, a summary of the scan made by a helper node, and publishes on /cmd_vel.

3. Your first nodes

3.1 The main() the lab gives you

Both assignments give you the same main() and tell you not to change it. It is worth reading line by line, because it explains what your own code must do.

def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = build_node()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()
  • rclpy.init() starts ROS 2 for this program.
  • build_node() is your function. It runs once. It creates the node, its publisher and its subscription, and returns the node. It does not call spin() itself.
  • rclpy.spin(node) keeps the program running. The ROS 2 tutorial says it spins the node "so its callbacks are called": while the node spins, the executor calls the function you registered with each message it takes from your subscription. In this setup callbacks run one at a time.
  • Once build_node() has returned and the program is inside try, the finally part destroys the node and calls rclpy.try_shutdown() when the program ends, for example when it is stopped. This cleans up ROS 2; it does not tell the robot to stop. try_shutdown() only shuts down if that has not already happened.

Key idea

Keep build_node() and your callbacks short. build_node() sets things up and returns; the waiting is done by rclpy.spin(), which calls your callback with each message it takes from the subscription. Use a timer for work that repeats on a schedule, and a subscription callback for work triggered by incoming messages. Do not write your own loop.

3.2 Example 1: a publisher with a timer

This node publishes a short text message on the topic /greeting every half second. It is adapted from the publisher in the ROS 2 Jazzy tutorial "Writing a simple publisher and subscriber (Python)", written in the build_node() style the lab uses.

ex1_hello_publisher.py

import rclpy
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import String


class HelloPublisher(Node):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('hello_publisher')
        # Message type, topic name, queue depth.
        self.publisher = self.create_publisher(String, '/greeting', 10)
        # Call self.publish_greeting every 0.5 seconds.
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.5, self.publish_greeting)
        self.count = 0

    def publish_greeting(self):
        message = String()
        message.data = f'Hello number {self.count}'
        self.publisher.publish(message)
        self.get_logger().info(f'Sent: {message.data}')
        self.count += 1


def build_node():
    return HelloPublisher()


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = build_node()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Example 1. Verified in ROS 2 Jazzy: it published "Hello number 0", "Hello number 1" and so on, twice per second.

  • create_publisher(String, '/greeting', 10) takes the message type, the topic name and a queue depth. The tutorial explains that the queue depth "is a required Quality of Service (QoS) setting that limits the amount of queued messages if a subscriber is not receiving them fast enough".
  • create_timer(0.5, self.publish_greeting) creates a timer with a period of 0.5 seconds. While the node is spinning, the executor runs publish_greeting when the timer is ready and the executor is free to run it. Note that the method is passed without parentheses: you hand ROS 2 the function, and ROS 2 calls it later.
  • publish() sends the message. get_logger().info() writes an INFO log line, which appears in the console when you run the node yourself on a computer with ROS 2 Jazzy installed.

3.3 Example 2: a subscription, written with plain functions

You do not have to write a class. Instead of a subclass of Node, you can call rclpy.create_node() to make the node and use an ordinary function as the callback. Assignment 1 accepts both styles.

ex2_listener_functions.py

import rclpy
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from std_msgs.msg import String


def build_node():
    node = rclpy.create_node('greeting_listener')

    def handle_greeting(message):
        # Runs once for each String the executor takes from this subscription.
        node.get_logger().info(f'Heard: {message.data}')

    # Pass the function itself: handle_greeting, not handle_greeting().
    node.create_subscription(String, '/greeting', handle_greeting, 10)
    return node


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = build_node()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Example 2. Verified in ROS 2 Jazzy together with Example 1.

When Examples 1 and 2 run at the same time, the listener logs each message its callback processes. Here is the matching pair of log lines for "Hello number 0" from the test run, publisher first. The middle number is a timestamp, which will differ for you. In this run the listener logged slightly before the publisher wrote its "Sent" line; that can happen because the publisher logs only after calling publish().

[INFO] [1795238155.424024988] [hello_publisher]: Sent: Hello number 0
[INFO] [1795238155.423794382] [greeting_listener]: Heard: Hello number 0

3.4 Queue depth is not a rate

The 10 in create_publisher and create_subscription is a history depth, not a frequency. The rclpy documentation describes this argument as "a QoSProfile or a history depth". Passing a number selects the history policy "keep last" with that depth and leaves the other QoS settings at their defaults. Each publisher and each subscription keeps its own history: when more messages are waiting than the depth allows, the oldest are dropped and only the newest are kept. It does not set a rate and does not guarantee that every message is processed. The publisher sets the publishing rate: in the lab, /scan is published about 12 times per second. A subscription may process fewer messages than were published.

The ROS 2 documentation lists the default settings as history "keep last" with a queue size of 10, reliability "reliable" and durability "volatile". QoS settings must be compatible for a publisher and a subscription to connect; for example, a reliable subscription does not receive from a best-effort publisher. In the lab, /scan and /flbr are published with depth 10 and the default settings, so a subscription with depth 10, as in the examples, matches them.

3.5 Common mistakes with nodes

MistakeWhat happensFix
create_subscription(..., self.handle_scan(), 10)The parentheses try to call the method during setup, without a scan. Python raises a TypeError and the subscription is never created.Pass the method itself: self.handle_scan.
return command inside the callbackROS 2 ignores what a callback returns, so nothing is sent.Call publisher.publish(command).
A while True: loop in build_node(), or time.sleep() in a callbackAn endless loop means build_node() never returns, so spin() never starts. A sleep in a callback holds up every other callback.Return from build_node() so that spin() can start. Keep callbacks short: use a timer for work that repeats on a schedule, and a subscription callback for work triggered by an incoming message.
build_node() forgets to return nodemain() receives None and fails when it tries to spin it.End build_node() with return node.
A typo in a topic name, such as /cmdvelNo error is shown. Your publisher does not connect to the robot base, which subscribes to /cmd_vel.Copy topic names exactly from the assignment.

4. Reading a LaserScan

4.1 The message

A laser range-finder, or LiDAR, measures distances in many directions in one sweep. Animation 4 shows the idea for a scanner with one beam turned by a rotating mirror: the beam sweeps across the room and a distance is measured in each direction. The bottom panel plots the measurements as points. A LaserScan message does not contain points: it holds the distances and the angles needed to place them (Section 4.2).

The lab's laser driver publishes each sweep as one sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan message. These are its fields, as printed by ROS 2 Jazzy:

FieldTypeMeaning (from the message definition)
headerstd_msgs/HeaderTime stamp and frame. The time stamp is the acquisition time of the first ray in the scan; frame_id names the frame the angles are measured in.
angle_minfloat32Start angle of the scan, in radians.
angle_maxfloat32End angle of the scan, in radians.
angle_incrementfloat32Angle between two neighbouring measurements, in radians.
time_incrementfloat32Time between measurements, in seconds.
scan_timefloat32Time between scans, in seconds.
range_minfloat32Minimum range value, in metres.
range_maxfloat32Maximum range value, in metres.
rangesfloat32[]The distances, in metres. Values below range_min or above range_max should be discarded.
intensitiesfloat32[]Signal strength in device-specific units; may be empty.

One callback receives one whole scan. scan.ranges holds all its distances. In ROS 2 Jazzy it is a Python array.array, which you index like a list: scan.ranges[0] is the first reading and len(scan.ranges) is the number of readings.

4.2 From an index to a direction

The message definition says that angles are measured around the positive Z axis of the scan's frame, counterclockwise if Z points up, and that zero is forward along the X axis. In the lab the laser's frame faces the same way as the robot, so a negative angle is to the robot's right and a positive angle to its left. Reading number i points in this direction:

angle_i = scan.angle_min + i * scan.angle_increment     # radians

Worked example A: a small scan

A scan has angle_min = -0.6, angle_increment = 0.2 and seven readings. The formula gives the angles −0.6, −0.4, −0.2, 0.0, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 radians for indexes 0 to 6. Index 3 is at 0.0 radians, straight ahead.

To go the other way, from a direction to an index, first write the direction in radians the way the scan measures angles (for example, −0.1 rather than 2π − 0.1). Never move a direction that lies outside the sweep onto its nearest end. Then solve the formula for i: i = (angle - angle_min) / angle_increment. This gives a fractional index. First check that it lies between 0 and len(scan.ranges) - 1. Because the fields are float32, a direction exactly at angle_min or angle_max can come out a tiny bit outside this range (for example 6.0000001 instead of 6), so allow a very small tolerance at the two ends; anything clearly outside means the direction is outside the sweep. Then round to the nearest whole number. For +0.33 radians, (0.33 + 0.6) / 0.2 = 4.65, so the nearest reading is index 5, at +0.4 radians. For +0.9 radians the fractional index is 7.5, which is past the last index (6): that direction is not in this scan. (These are the stated values; the message stores them as float32, so computed angles can differ in the last digits.)

Worked example B: a scan like the lab's

The lab's laser sweeps from −135° on the robot's right to +135° on its left in 3° steps, which gives 91 readings. Index 0 is at −135°, index 90 is at +135°, and the middle index, 91 // 2 = 45, is at 0°: straight ahead.

The Assignment 1 handout states the same fact. Taking the middle index works because the scan is symmetric (angle_min equals -angle_max), evenly spaced and has an odd number of readings, so its middle reading is at zero. For any other scan, compute the angles with the formula instead of assuming.

Radians, not degrees

Every angle in a LaserScan is in radians. To convert in Python, use math.radians(degrees) and math.degrees(radians). 3 degrees is about 0.0524 radians.

One radian is the angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius, so a full turn is 2π radians, about 6.283, and 1 radian is about 57.3 degrees. Animation 5 shows this.

Try it: change the scan's start angle, step and size, then pick a reading to see its direction, or type a direction to find its reading.

4.3 Special values: +inf, -inf and NaN

A reading is not always a plain distance. REP 117, the ROS standard for distance measurements, defines three special values:

ValueMeaning in REP 117Python test
+infNo detection within the sensor's range for that reading (REP 117: "likely no object within range").math.isinf(d) and d > 0
-infSomething was detected, but too close to measure.math.isinf(d) and d < 0
NaNAn erroneous or invalid measurement: no useful distance.math.isnan(d)

math.isfinite(d) is True only for an ordinary number, so it is False for all three special values. Combined with the range limits from the message, it picks out the finite readings inside the limits:

usable = math.isfinite(d) and scan.range_min <= d <= scan.range_max

NaN behaves strangely in Python

For Python floats, ==, <, >, <= and >= with NaN are always False, and != is always True. These results were checked in Python 3.12:

ExpressionResult
math.nan == math.nanFalse, so never test with == math.nan; use math.isnan()
math.nan < 0.5False
math.nan > 0.5False
math.nan != math.nanTrue
min([0.5, math.nan])0.5
min([math.nan, 0.5])nan: the same numbers in a different order give a different answer
math.inf > 4.0True
-math.inf < 0.1True: infinities compare as expected

Because of this, handle NaN yourself before comparing or taking a minimum, and decide in advance what an unknown reading should mean for your robot.

4.4 Example 3: counting the usable readings

This node counts, in each scan it processes, the finite readings inside the range limits, and publishes the count. It shows the whole pattern of a scan callback. The count is a diagnostic: it does not say whether the robot's path is clear.

ex3_scan_return_counter.py

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.node import Node
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan
from std_msgs.msg import Int32


class ScanReturnCounter(Node):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('scan_return_counter')
        self.count_publisher = self.create_publisher(Int32, '/usable_return_count', 10)
        self.create_subscription(LaserScan, '/scan', self.handle_scan, 10)

    def handle_scan(self, scan):
        count = 0
        for distance in scan.ranges:
            # NaN and both infinities fail isfinite(); the limits come from the message.
            if math.isfinite(distance) and scan.range_min <= distance <= scan.range_max:
                count += 1
        self.count_publisher.publish(Int32(data=count))


def build_node():
    return ScanReturnCounter()


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = build_node()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Example 3. Verified in ROS 2 Jazzy with the scan in the scenario below: it published 3 for every scan.

Scenario: reading one scan by hand

A scan has range_min = 0.10, range_max = 4.00, angle_min = -0.6 and angle_increment = 0.2. Here is how each reading is treated:

IndexAngle (rad)ReadingTreatment
0−0.6+infNot usable: nothing detected in range
1−0.41.2Usable
2−0.2NaNNot usable: invalid measurement
30.00.04Not usable: below range_min, so discarded
4+0.20.8Usable
5+0.42.4Usable
6+0.6-infNot usable: too close to measure

Three readings are usable, so the node publishes 3. A count of 0 would not mean the way is clear: it would only mean there were no finite readings inside the limits. Neither infinity is a finite distance, but they mean different things: the +inf at index 0 reports no detection within range, while the -inf at index 6 reports something too close to measure. Keep the meaning of a reading separate from the action your program takes: follow the handout for the cases it specifies, and if a case matters that the handout does not cover, ask before assuming.

4.5 Common mistakes with scans

  • Mixing degrees and radians, for example comparing an angle with 90.
  • Assuming len(scan.ranges) // 2 points straight ahead for every scan. Check the angle with the formula.
  • Using a negative index by accident. In Python scan.ranges[-1] is not an error when the scan has readings: it is the last reading. In the lab's scan that is the reading at +135°, on the robot's far left. (Only an empty ranges raises an IndexError.)
  • Treating every special value the same way. +inf (nothing in range) and -inf (too close) mean opposite things.
  • Testing for NaN with ==.

5. Commanding motion with Twist

5.1 The message

In the lab, the robot's velocity request is sent on /cmd_vel as a geometry_msgs/msg/Twist message. ROS 2 Jazzy prints its definition as two vectors, each with three float64 numbers:

Vector3  linear      # x, y, z
Vector3  angular     # x, y, z

linear is a velocity along each axis and angular is a turning rate around each axis. The lab's robot can only drive forward or backward and turn, so it uses two of the six numbers, linear.x and angular.z; leave the other four at zero. A plain Twist has no header and no time stamp.

5.2 Units, axes and signs (REP 103)

REP 103, the ROS standard for units and coordinate frames, fixes three things you need:

  • Units are SI. Lengths are in metres and angles in radians, so linear.x is in metres per second and angular.z is in radians per second.
  • Axes on the robot's body frame. x points forward, y points left and z points up.
  • Right-handed frames. With z pointing up, a positive rotation around z is counterclockwise when seen from above. So positive angular.z turns the robot left and negative angular.z turns it right.

A quick way to remember the sign is the right-hand grip rule in Figure 6: point the thumb of your right hand along the +z axis (up), and your fingers curl the way a positive rotation turns, which is counterclockwise when seen from above.

5.3 Reading and writing commands

(linear.x, angular.z)What the robot is asked to do
(0.15, 0.0)Drive straight forward at 0.15 m/s
(-0.10, 0.0)Drive straight backward at 0.10 m/s
(0.0, +0.4)Turn left on the spot at 0.4 rad/s (about 22.9 degrees per second)
(0.0, -0.4)Turn right on the spot at 0.4 rad/s
(0.15, +0.4)Drive forward while curving to the left
(0.0, 0.0)Zero velocity: stop

A Twist on /cmd_vel is a request, not a measurement. How closely a real robot follows it depends on its controller limits, acceleration, wheel grip and any command timeout.

Try it: set linear.x, angular.z and a time to see where the ideal unicycle model takes the robot.

5.4 How the wheels carry out a Twist

The lab's simulation moves the robot with the unicycle model, which describes a differential-drive robot from the Locomotion topic: two driven wheels on one axle. In the ideal model, with no wheel slip, let L be the distance between the centres of the two wheels and v_right and v_left the speeds of the two wheels along the ground, in m/s. The forward speed v (linear.x) and the turning rate ω (angular.z) come from them: v = (v_right + v_left) / 2 and ω = (v_right − v_left) / L.

Figure 9 shows a real robot of this kind, the TurtleBot3 Burger, a small robot widely used for teaching ROS. Its two wheels are each driven by their own motor, and the round sensor on top is a 360-degree laser distance sensor (the lab's laser covers 270 degrees). Figure 10 shows the wheel layout of such a robot as a diagram, seen from above.

Solving for the wheels gives v_right = v + ω·L/2 and v_left = v − ω·L/2. For example, with L = 0.30 m:

  • v = 0.15 m/s and ω = +0.4 rad/s give v_right = 0.21 m/s and v_left = 0.09 m/s. The right wheel is faster, so the robot curves to the left.
  • v = 0 and ω = +0.4 rad/s give v_right = +0.06 m/s and v_left = −0.06 m/s. The wheels turn in opposite directions and the robot turns on the spot.

Try it: enter a forward speed, a turning rate and a wheel separation to see each wheel's ground speed.

5.5 Example 4: turn for about three seconds, then send zeros

This node needs no sensor. A timer with a 0.1 s period publishes a command on each callback: the first 30 callbacks ask the robot to turn left on the spot at 0.4 rad/s, and every later callback sends all zeros. With ideal timing, about 3 s pass from the first turn command to the first zero command.

ex4_timed_pivot.py

import rclpy
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.node import Node


class TimedPivot(Node):
    """Send 30 turn-left commands, then keep sending zero commands."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('timed_pivot')
        self.publisher = self.create_publisher(Twist, '/cmd_vel', 10)
        self.ticks = 0
        self.timer = self.create_timer(0.1, self.send_command)  # 10 commands per second

    def send_command(self):
        command = Twist()            # a fresh message: every field starts at 0.0
        if self.ticks < 30:          # the first 30 timer callbacks (about 3 s)
            command.angular.z = 0.4  # rad/s, positive = counterclockwise = left
        # From callback 31 on nothing is set, so every field stays 0.0: zero velocity.
        self.publisher.publish(command)
        self.ticks += 1


def build_node():
    return TimedPivot()


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = build_node()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Example 4. Verified in ROS 2 Jazzy: 30 commands with angular.z = 0.4, then only zero commands, with linear.x = 0.0 throughout.

  • Each call makes a fresh Twist(), so every field starts at 0.0. If you reuse one message object, a value set earlier stays in it unless you overwrite it.
  • On the lab's /cmd_vel, a Twist with all zeros explicitly asks for zero velocity. Sending nothing is not the same: it makes no new request, and what the robot does then depends on the robot base. To stop, publish zeros.

Common mistakes with Twist

  • Setting angular.x or angular.y instead of angular.z. A ground robot turns around z.
  • Writing a turning rate in degrees per second. 30 in angular.z asks for 30 radians per second, about 4.8 full turns every second.
  • Getting the sign backwards: positive angular.z is a left turn.

6. Custom messages: the course's Flbr

Any project can define its own message types. This course defines rse_msgs/msg/Flbr, used in Assignment 2. A helper node in the lab turns each scan into four numbers, one for each direction, and publishes them on /flbr. This is the complete definition:

# Closest usable obstacle distance in each sector.
# Distances use meters.
# NaN indicates that the sector is unavailable.

std_msgs/Header header

float32 front
float32 left
float32 back
float32 right

You read the fields directly: msg.front, msg.left, msg.back and msg.right. The meaning of this message comes from the course, not from REP 117: a value is the closest usable distance in that sector, in metres, and NaN means the helper has no usable distance for that sector. How a controller should treat NaN is a separate rule, given in the assignment.

The lab's helper puts a reading in a sector only if its direction is strictly less than 45° from the sector's centre. The helper works out each reading's direction in whole degrees, −135 + 3 × index, so the lab's laser covers exactly −135° to +135°: those two end readings lie exactly on the back sector's edges and are left out, and no other reading is inside it. So msg.back is always NaN in the lab. A sector name does not mean the whole sector was seen.

6.1 Example 5: a sector report

For each Flbr message its callback processes, this node publishes one line of text. It shows how to treat a NaN field: say it is unavailable, rather than printing it or pretending it is a number.

ex5_sector_report.py

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.node import Node
from rse_msgs.msg import Flbr
from std_msgs.msg import String


def describe(name, distance):
    if math.isnan(distance):
        return f'{name} unavailable'
    return f'{name} {distance:.2f} m'


class SectorReport(Node):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('sector_report')
        self.report_publisher = self.create_publisher(String, '/sector_report', 10)
        self.create_subscription(Flbr, '/flbr', self.handle_flbr, 10)

    def handle_flbr(self, msg):
        parts = [
            describe('front', msg.front),
            describe('left', msg.left),
            describe('back', msg.back),
            describe('right', msg.right),
        ]
        self.report_publisher.publish(String(data=' | '.join(parts)))


def build_node():
    return SectorReport()


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = build_node()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Example 5. Verified in ROS 2 Jazzy.

For a test message with the values in Figure 11 it published exactly this line:

front 1.10 m | left unavailable | back 0.80 m | right 1.60 m

Good to know: float32

The Flbr and LaserScan distances are float32. Many decimals cannot be stored exactly in that format: 0.40 sent in a float32 field arrives as a value Python shows as 0.4000000059604645, slightly larger than the Python number 0.40, so the test reading <= 0.40 is False for that reading. Values such as 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 are stored exactly. So for a limit that includes its end, test just below, exactly at and just above it, using values sent through the message field, not only Python numbers, and check that a reading exactly at the limit takes the branch your rule says.

7. From a rule to code

Assignments state their rules in words. Before writing code, turn the rule into a table of cases. A good table covers values just below, at and just above every limit, every special value, and any tie.

7.1 Scenario: a low-battery warning

Robots report their battery with the standard message sensor_msgs/msg/BatteryState. Its field percentage is the charge "on 0 to 1 range", and the message definition says it is NaN when unmeasured. Rule: "Warn when the battery is at 25% or below. If the charge is not measured, warn as well." The words "or below" mean that exactly 25% warns, so the comparison is <=, not <.

percentageWarn?Why
0.24YesBelow 25%
0.25YesExactly at the limit: "or below" includes it
0.26NoAbove the limit
1.00NoFully charged
NaNYesNot measured: the rule says to warn

7.2 Example 6: the warning node

The decision is kept in a plain function, low_battery(), separate from the ROS 2 parts. The node only calls it: one message in, one message out.

ex6_battery_warning.py

import math

import rclpy
from rclpy.executors import ExternalShutdownException
from rclpy.node import Node
from sensor_msgs.msg import BatteryState
from std_msgs.msg import Bool

LOW_BATTERY = 0.25  # 25 %, on the message's 0 to 1 scale


def low_battery(percentage, limit=LOW_BATTERY):
    """True when the charge is at or below the limit, or not measured (NaN)."""
    if math.isnan(percentage):
        return True
    return percentage <= limit


class BatteryWarning(Node):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('battery_warning')
        self.warning_publisher = self.create_publisher(Bool, '/low_battery', 10)
        self.create_subscription(BatteryState, '/battery_state', self.handle_battery, 10)

    def handle_battery(self, msg):
        # One message in, one message out.
        self.warning_publisher.publish(Bool(data=low_battery(msg.percentage)))


def build_node():
    return BatteryWarning()


def main(args=None):
    rclpy.init(args=args)
    node = build_node()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except (KeyboardInterrupt, ExternalShutdownException):
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Example 6. Verified in ROS 2 Jazzy: for the five values in the table it published True, True, False, False, True.

Because low_battery() is plain Python, you can check every row of the table without a robot. The test imports the node's file, so run it on a computer with ROS 2 Jazzy installed. Like the other examples, it is a standalone program, not part of the lab app. It checks the decision, not the messaging:

test_low_battery.py

import math

from ex6_battery_warning import low_battery

assert low_battery(0.24) is True
assert low_battery(0.25) is True   # "at or below" includes the limit
assert low_battery(0.26) is False
assert low_battery(1.00) is False
assert low_battery(math.nan) is True   # not measured counts as low
print('all low_battery checks passed')

A test for the decision function. Verified: it prints "all low_battery checks passed".

7.3 Ties and missing cases

A rule that chooses between two options must say what happens when they are equal. "Go to the nearer charging station" does not say which station to pick when both are 2.0 m away. In an assignment, follow the handout's rules exactly. If a case such as a tie or an unavailable reading is not covered, ask before assuming what the grader expects, and add the case to your table.

8. Before you start the assignments

One message in, one fresh command

In both assignments, for each message your callback processes, it publishes one command, decided from that message alone. The node does not need to remember earlier messages. While the messages keep showing the same situation, the callback keeps sending the same command, and repeating a stop command many times is normal. Different readings can call for the same command: two different short distances can both mean stop. When a later message calls for a different action, the same rule sends a different command. Also keep two kinds of rule apart. Example 3 counts only finite readings inside the range limits. It leaves +inf out because +inf reports no detection within range, not a finite distance; that does not make it an invalid reading, and the count does not decide how the robot should move. A rule that decides how to move asks a different question, and must say what +inf means for motion; follow REP 117 and the assignment handout.

Checklist

Check that you can answer yes to each question:

  • Does build_node() create the publisher and the subscription, then return the node, without looping or sleeping?
  • Is the callback passed without parentheses?
  • Does the callback publish a command for every message it receives?
  • For a LaserScan, have you checked with the formula which index points in the direction you need? For Flbr, do you use the right named field?
  • Do you handle each special value (+inf, -inf, NaN) that your assignment's rule covers, and have you asked about any case it does not cover?
  • Are your speeds in m/s and turning rates in rad/s, with positive angular.z for left?
  • Does every command start from a fresh Twist() (or overwrite every field you use)? Do you set linear.x to 0.0 to stop driving forward, and send an all-zero Twist only when the rule asks for no motion at all?
  • Have you written a table of cases, with values at and around every limit?

The Simulate button in the lab replays what your node makes the robot do. Use it to compare the robot's behaviour with your table.
